_source: Documented herb-drug interaction pairs from: Natural Medicines Comprehensive Database, WHO Herbal Safety Monographs, Stargrove et al. 'Herb, Nutrient, and Drug Interactions' (2008), Memorial Sloan Kettering About Herbs database, and Cochrane systematic reviews.
_note: herbName and drugName are lowercase normalized. drugName may refer to a specific drug or a class. Multiple entries per herb cover different drug classes.

interactions.description: Curcumin (the active compound in turmeric) inhibits platelet aggregation and has mild anticoagulant activity. Combined use with warfarin may potentiate anticoagulation, increasing bleeding risk. INR monitoring is advised if concurrent use cannot be avoided. Sources: Natural Medicines Database, multiple case reports.

Turmeric/curcumin inhibits thromboxane synthesis and platelet aggregation through similar but additive pathways to aspirin. Combined use can increase bleeding risk, particularly in patients with gastrointestinal vulnerabilities or on dual antiplatelet therapy.

Curcumin has demonstrated antiplatelet activity via inhibition of arachidonic acid metabolism. Concurrent use with clopidogrel may additively inhibit platelet function, raising the risk of bruising, prolonged bleeding, or haemorrhage.

Turmeric has demonstrated modest blood pressure-lowering effects in clinical studies. Combined use with antihypertensive drugs (ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, ARBs) may produce additive hypotension, particularly in higher-dose supplementation.

Curcumin is the bioactive constituent of turmeric. It inhibits platelet aggregation and coagulation cascade enzymes. Combined use with warfarin is associated with raised INR and increased bleeding risk in published case reports.

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) contains gingerols and shogaols that inhibit thromboxane synthetase and platelet aggregation. Combined use with warfarin has been associated with raised INR and spontaneous bruising in case reports. Monitor INR closely.

Ginger has antiplatelet properties that may be additive with aspirin's COX-1 inhibition. Combined use at high ginger supplement doses may mildly increase bleeding time. Most relevant in post-operative patients or those with gastric mucosal fragility.

Clinical studies have shown ginger can modestly reduce fasting blood glucose. Combined use with antidiabetic drugs (metformin, sulfonylureas, insulin) may have additive hypoglycaemic effects, increasing the risk of low blood sugar.

Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) has documented anxiolytic and mild CNS depressant properties (GABA-A receptor modulation). Combined use with benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or sedating antihistamines may produce additive central nervous system depression, drowsiness, and psychomotor impairment.

Ashwagandha has been shown in clinical trials to stimulate thyroid hormone synthesis (T3/T4 elevation). Combined use with levothyroxine or thyroid replacement therapy may produce thyrotoxic effects (palpitations, anxiety, weight loss). Thyroid function should be monitored.

Ashwagandha has demonstrated immunostimulatory activity (NK cell activation, macrophage stimulation). This may antagonize the therapeutic effect of immunosuppressive drugs used post-transplant or in autoimmune conditions (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, corticosteroids).

Allicin and ajoene in high-dose garlic supplements inhibit platelet aggregation and thromboxane formation. Documented cases of spontaneous retroperitoneal and epidural hematomas when combined with warfarin.

High-dose garlic supplements significantly induce CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, leading to markedly reduced plasma concentrations of HIV antiretroviral drugs (saquinavir reduced by ~50% in pharmacokinetic studies). This may lead to therapeutic failure and viral resistance.
Ginkgolide B is a potent antagonist of platelet-activating factor (PAF). Concurrent use with warfarin has produced spontaneous hyphema, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and hematoma. Severe bleeding risk.
Dual antiplatelet inhibition through cyclooxygenase blockade (aspirin) and PAF antagonism (ginkgo) dramatically elevates spontaneous hemorrhagic risk, including ocular bleeding.

Ginkgo biloba may lower seizure threshold and reduce the efficacy of antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine), possibly through induction of drug-metabolising enzymes. Case reports of seizure recurrence in controlled epilepsy exist.
Valeriana officinalis enhances GABAergic transmission. Combined use with benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or sedatives causes excessive daytime sedation and respiratory depression.

Valerian may have pharmacodynamic synergy with alprazolam (Xanax) and other benzodiazepines via GABA-A receptor modulation. This may potentiate sedation, memory impairment, and psychomotor depression. Avoid concurrent use without clinical supervision.

Echinacea is an immunostimulant and may counteract the therapeutic intent of immunosuppressive drugs (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azathioprine) used in transplant patients or autoimmune disease. Risk of graft rejection or disease flare with concurrent use.

Echinacea preparations have been rarely associated with hepatotoxicity. Combined use with other hepatotoxic drugs (statins, isoniazid, methotrexate) may increase liver enzyme elevation risk. Liver function monitoring is recommended in long-term use.
Panax ginseng has been shown in controlled clinical trials to decrease warfarin blood levels and significantly reduce INR, raising the danger of arterial thrombosis and stroke.
Ginsenosides enhance pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion and peripheral glucose uptake, which can additively cause severe hypoglycemia when combined with metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin.
Licorice-induced sodium and water retention elevates systemic vascular resistance, neutralizing blood pressure control from antihypertensive medications.
Licorice-induced hypokalemia profoundly sensitizes cardiac myocytes to digoxin toxicity, triggering fatal arrhythmias and heart block.

Hypericum perforatum inhibits reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. Combined use with SSRIs, SNRIs, or TCAs significantly increases the risk of severe Serotonin Syndrome (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rigidity).

St. John's Wort is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP3A4 enzymes and intestinal P-glycoprotein. It accelerates estrogen and progestin clearance, resulting in breakthrough bleeding and unintended pregnancy.

St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) strongly induces CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 enzymes as well as P-glycoprotein. Concurrent use leads to accelerated warfarin clearance, a precipitous drop in INR, and a high risk of catastrophic thromboembolic stroke or deep vein thrombosis.
St. John's wort induces intestinal P-glycoprotein, reducing digoxin bioavailability by 25-35% and causing loss of ventricular rate control or heart failure exacerbation.

Hyperforin in St. John's wort potently induces intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, reducing cyclosporine or tacrolimus blood levels by 50-70%. This has caused acute organ transplant rejection in numerous documented clinical cases.
Green tea contains significant quantities of Vitamin K1 and EGCG. Large consumption or concentrated extract intake dramatically antagonizes warfarin, dropping INR and precipitating thromboembolism.

Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) inhibits organic anion-transporting polypeptide (OATP1A2/OATP1B1), significantly decreasing the intestinal absorption and bioavailability of beta-blockers like nadolol and atenolol.
EGCG modulates hepatic OATP transport and CYP3A4 metabolism, altering plasma concentrations of atorvastatin and simvastatin.
Coenzyme Q10 shares chemical structural homology with Vitamin K (menaquinone). It can diminish warfarin's anticoagulant efficacy, causing sub-therapeutic INR and clot risk.
CoQ10 has mild intrinsic vasodilatory and blood pressure-lowering properties. Concomitant use with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or CCBs can cause additive hypotension.

Melatonin combined with benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam) or Z-drugs (zolpidem) results in profound central nervous system depression, impaired psychomotor performance, and increased risk of nocturnal falls.
Exogenous melatonin may impair nocturnal blood pressure dip and has been reported to interfere with the efficacy of calcium channel blockers (nifedipine).
High soluble galactomannan fiber and 4-hydroxyisoleucine in fenugreek seeds stimulate insulin secretion and slow glucose absorption, causing acute hypoglycemia when combined with antidiabetic drugs.
Fenugreek contains natural coumarin derivatives that exert additive anticoagulant properties, elevating bleeding risk and prolonging prothrombin time.
Holy Basil (Ocimum sanctum / Tulsi) exhibits antiplatelet and anticoagulant properties via cyclooxygenase inhibition, synergistically increasing bleeding risks with warfarin, aspirin, or clopidogrel.
Tulsi has documented hypoglycemic action. When combined with oral antidiabetics (metformin, glimepiride), monitor for sudden blood glucose drops.

Glycyrrhizin in licorice inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, inducing apparent mineralocorticoid excess (pseudoaldosteronism) causing severe hypokalemia, sodium retention, and ventricular arrhythmia with loop diuretics (furosemide).

Piper methysticum (Kava) is strongly hepatotoxic and depletes hepatic glutathione reserves. Concurrent use with paracetamol (acetaminophen) significantly accelerates hepatic injury and acute liver failure risk.
Ginkgolide B is a potent platelet-activating factor (PAF) antagonist. When co-administered with NSAIDs like ibuprofen, multiple clinical reports document spontaneous hyphema and subdural hematomas.

Marked induction of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein by St. John's wort leads to subtherapeutic immunosuppressant levels and catastrophic allograft rejection in renal, liver, and cardiac transplant recipients.
Enzyme induction by St. John's wort accelerates the hepatic metabolism of ethinyl estradiol and progestins, causing breakthrough bleeding and documented unintended pregnancies.

St. John's wort inhibits synaptosomal reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. When combined with SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram) or SNRIs, it precipitates severe, potentially fatal Serotonin Syndrome (hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability).
Additive central serotonergic stimulation can trigger Serotonin Syndrome characterized by agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, and altered mental status.
Severe risk of Serotonin Syndrome due to combined synaptic serotonin reuptake inhibition and long active metabolite half-lives.
Synergistic serotonergic toxicity resulting in dangerous hyperthermia, myoclonus, and autonomic collapse.

Combined 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism from triptans (sumatriptan, zolmitriptan) and serotonergic elevation from St. John's wort substantially raises the risk of coronary vasoconstriction and serotonin syndrome.
Both tramadol and St. John's wort inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; combining them greatly elevates risk of seizures and life-threatening Serotonin Syndrome.
CYP3A4 induction by St. John's wort reduces atorvastatin and simvastatin plasma concentrations, compromising cardiovascular LDL reduction.
St. John's wort significantly increases hepatic clearance of simvastatin, reducing lipid-lowering efficacy and arterial plaque stabilization.
Induction of CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 by St. John's wort lowers theophylline plasma levels by up to 50%, precipitating severe bronchospasm in asthma and COPD.
Induces clearance of carbamazepine, phenytoin, and phenobarbital, resulting in subtherapeutic anticonvulsant levels and breakthrough epileptic seizures.
Induces CYP3A4 clearance of alprazolam and midazolam, significantly diminishing anxiolytic and sedative therapeutic efficacy.
Combining ADP P2Y12 receptor blockade with ginkgolide PAF inhibition results in profound platelet dysfunction and increased major bleeding events.
Direct factor Xa inhibition combined with ginkgo's antiplatelet action substantially increases gastrointestinal and intracranial bleeding vulnerability.
Additive antithrombotic mechanisms heighten the probability of major hemorrhagic complications. Co-administration is strongly discouraged.
Ginkgo additively impairs hemostasis when taken with ibuprofen, diclofenac, or naproxen, increasing gastrointestinal mucosal bleeding and ulcer risk.
Ginkgo seeds and unpurified extracts contain ginkgotoxin (4-O-methylpyridoxine), an antivitamin B6 compound that impairs GABA synthesis and lowers seizure threshold, precipitating convulsions.
Ginkgotoxin antagonizes the neuroprotective action of valproic acid, leading to loss of seizure control and status epilepticus in epileptic patients.
Co-administration has been reported to induce excessive sedation and reversible coma through synergistic central nervous system depression.
Ginkgo may stimulate hepatic metabolic clearance of insulin and oral hypoglycemic agents, causing erratic glycemic fluctuations in type 2 diabetic patients.
Additive platelet inhibition through cyclooxygenase and thromboxane pathways elevates bleeding time, bruising, and perioperative hemorrhagic risk.
Enhanced platelet anti-aggregatory activity raises vulnerability to occult gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Discontinue high-dose garlic 7-10 days before surgery.
Garlic extract significantly reduces plasma concentrations of saquinavir and other HIV protease inhibitors by approximately 50%, predisposing to therapeutic failure and viral resistance.
Garlic stimulates endothelial nitric oxide and hydrogen sulfide production, which can cause additive hypotension when combined with ACE inhibitors or calcium channel blockers.
Combining Panax ginseng with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) has resulted in severe headaches, tremors, insomnia, and manic-like psychomotor agitation.
Ginseng stimulates macrophage and natural killer cell activity, potentially antagonizing the therapeutic effects of corticosteroids, methotrexate, or tofacitinib.
Ginseng exerts biphasic cardiovascular effects (low doses increase BP, high doses decrease BP), creating erratic blood pressure control in hypertensive patients.
Curcumin inhibits factor Xa, thrombin, and platelet aggregation. Concomitant use with DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) increases systemic bleeding risk.
Curcumin is an active iron chelator that binds ferric iron in the gut, significantly reducing dietary and supplemental iron absorption and worsening iron-deficiency anemia.
Curcumin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, causing unpredictable spikes in tacrolimus blood levels and heightened nephrotoxicity risk.
Curcumin suppresses cyclooxygenase-2 and thromboxane synthesis; combined with aspirin, this synergistic antiplatelet effect raises bleeding and GI irritation risk.
Curcumin activates AMPK pathways similarly to metformin, leading to additive glycemic reduction and potential mild hypoglycemia.

Glycyrrhizin inhibits renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, resulting in mineralocorticoid excess with severe potassium wasting. Combined with furosemide or hydrochlorothiazide, it causes life-threatening hypokalemia and cardiac arrhythmias.
Severe synergistic potassium depletion resulting in muscle paralysis, QT interval prolongation, and torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia.

Licorice-induced pseudoaldosteronism triggers massive renal sodium retention and hypervolemia, directly counteracting ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and calcium channel blockers and causing severe refractory hypertension.
Licorice-induced hypokalemia sensitizes the myocardial Na/K-ATPase to digoxin, precipitating lethal digoxin toxicity, heart block, and ventricular arrhythmias even at normal digoxin serum levels.
Licorice impairs the metabolic conversion of cortisol to inactive cortisone, potentiating systemic corticosteroid exposure, hypertension, fluid retention, and adrenal suppression.
Licorice accelerates hepatic clearance of warfarin via CYP2C9 induction, resulting in subtherapeutic INR and thrombosis risk.
Kavalactones potentiate GABA-A receptor binding. Concurrent use with benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or barbiturates causes severe stupor, prolonged lethargy, and respiratory depression.
Synergistic central nervous system depression. Documented clinical cases of semicomatose lethargy requiring emergency hospitalization.
Kava extracts deplete hepatic glutathione and inhibit multiple P450 enzymes. Combined with paracetamol, this dramatically increases NAPQI-mediated acute liver necrosis.
Additive hepatotoxic burden. Concomitant use increases serum transaminases and predisposing to drug-induced liver injury (DILI).
Kavalactones antagonize central dopamine receptors, directly reversing the therapeutic effects of levodopa and acutely worsening Parkinsonian tremors and akinesia.
Valerenic acid stimulates GABA synthesis and inhibits GABA reuptake. Combined with benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam) or zolpidem, it causes pronounced daytime somnolence and cognitive slowing.
Additive sedative-hypnotic CNS depression resulting in severe motor incoordination, sleepwalking, and daytime psychomotor impairment.
Profound additive CNS depression and impaired reaction time. Patients must avoid alcohol when taking valerian supplements.
Additive muscle relaxation and central somnolence with baclofen, thiocolchicoside, or tizanidine, increasing fall risk.
Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) potently inhibits intestinal OATP1A2 uptake transporters, reducing nadolol bioavailability by up to 85% and causing complete loss of beta-blocker efficacy.
EGCG directly binds the boronic acid moiety of bortezomib (Velcade), completely neutralizing its proteasome inhibitory anti-myeloma activity in clinical oncology.
High-dose green tea extract has been linked to idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; concurrent statin therapy increases risk of elevated hepatic transaminases.
Tea catechins bind non-heme iron to form insoluble complexes, reducing iron bioavailability by over 70% and aggravating microcytic anemia.
Silymarin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity and decreases gluconeogenesis. When combined with metformin or sulfonylureas, close glucose monitoring is recommended to prevent hypoglycemia.
Silymarin stimulates CYP-mediated metabolism, accelerating clearance of metronidazole and potentially compromising treatment of anaerobic bacterial infections.
Dual 5-alpha-reductase inhibition without clinical additive efficacy; increases likelihood of antiandrogenic adverse effects including erectile dysfunction and gynecomastia.
Isolated clinical reports of prolonged bleeding time and INR elevation. Monitor coagulation parameters during initiation or discontinuation.

Echinacea stimulates macrophage, tumor necrosis factor, and interleukin activity, directly counteracting the therapeutic intentions of immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, tofacitinib, systemic steroids).
Inhibits CYP1A2, increasing caffeine half-life and predisposing to palpitations, jitteriness, and insomnia.
Cranberry juice and concentrated capsules inhibit CYP2C9 metabolism of S-warfarin. Multiple cases of marked INR elevation and fatal bleeding have been documented.
Berberine in goldenseal strongly inhibits P-glycoprotein, dramatically reducing digoxin efflux and causing potentially lethal digitalis toxicity.
Potent inhibition of CYP3A4 increases midazolam and triazolam exposure by more than 150%, inducing prolonged sedation and respiratory depression.
Berberine and metformin both act on AMPK pathways and organic cation transporters (OCT); combined use may cause additive gastrointestinal distress and hypoglycemia.
Parthenolide in feverfew inhibits platelet aggregation and serotonin release from platelets, adding to the anticoagulant hazard of warfarin.
Synergistic inhibition of prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis elevates mucosal and surgical bleeding risks.
Chronic or excessive use of senna anthraquinone laxatives causes severe potassium wasting. Hypokalemia greatly sensitizes the myocardium to fatal digoxin-induced arrhythmias.
Additive renal and intestinal potassium loss creates profound hypokalemia, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and neuromuscular weakness.
Yohimbine is a potent central and peripheral alpha-2 adrenergic antagonist that releases massive norepinephrine surges, causing dangerous spikes in blood pressure and tachyarrhythmias.
Combined use with tricyclic antidepressants or MAOIs triggers severe hypertensive crisis, tremors, panic agitation, and cardiac arrhythmias.
Additive central hypnotic effect with benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or sedating antihistamines, causing marked daytime drowsiness, dizziness, and cognitive impairment.
Melatonin may have mild antiplatelet effects and immune-modulating actions that can occasionally alter coagulation parameters in anticoagulated patients.
